SleeperGem malicious gem artifacts written to gems path (git_credential_manager / Dendreo / fastlane-plugin) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation of the three SleeperGem-compromised gems by watching for their package names written under a RubyGems gems/specifications directory. Catches both direct install of git_credential_manager and transitive pull-in via the trojanised Dendreo dependency. Rationale: Uses the three exact gem names named in the article/second sources. Requiring a gems/ or specifications/ path element removes coincidental filename collisions (e.g. a source repo literally called git_credential_manager) and keys on the RubyGems install layout. Dendreo is anchored with the '-<version>' gem-directory pattern to avoid matching the company name in unrelated docs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/sleepergem-attack-targets-ruby-ecosystem-with-malicious-gems
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately used the real (pre-compromise) Dendreo gem pinned to a clean version
  • Mirror/offline gem cache syncs that pull the full index including these names
  • Security tooling that stages the malicious samples for analysis
  • A developer cloning the legit git-credential-manager project (dash-form, not underscore) — excluded by underscore match
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("defender","mssense.exe") or FolderPath has "MpEnginedb")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the gem's .gemspec / lib load hook to confirm the git.disroot.org fetch and the CI-skip check, and identify the installed version (2.8.0-2.8.3 for git_credential_manager). 2) Contain: gem uninstall the three packages fleet-wide, pin known-good versions, and rotate any credentials (esp. git credential helpers) touched on affected laptops. 3) Hunt: correlate install time with subsequent git.disroot.org network hits and ruby->shell spawns; audit Gemfile.lock in CI/repos for the malicious dependency edge from Dendreo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "gems" or FolderPath has "specifications")
| where FolderPath has_any ("git_credential_manager","fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab") or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]Dendreo-\d"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "gems" or TargetFilePath has "specifications")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("git_credential_manager","fastlane-plugin-run_tests_firebase_testlab") or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]Dendreo-\d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SleeperGem Unix persistence: cron/systemd/LaunchAgent write by Ruby-descended shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the SleeperGem post-exploitation stage on developer laptops where the native daemon establishes persistence via cron jobs and systemd services (and LaunchAgents/Daemons on macOS), written by a Ruby-family or shell process. Corroborated by The Hacker News reporting of cron+systemd persistence after CI-evasion. Rationale: Targets the cron+systemd (and macOS Launch) persistence that second-source reporting (The Hacker News) attributes to the SleeperGem native daemon, scoped to a Ruby/shell writer to reflect the gem->/bin/sh->daemon chain. High FP by nature (config-management tooling writes these paths), so shipped as hunting with a Ruby/shell ancestry constraint. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/sleepergem-uses-three-malicious.html
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt agents (often Ruby) writing systemd units and cron entries
  • Developer install scripts (curl|sh) that register a systemd service or LaunchAgent
  • Homebrew/rbenv post-install hooks creating LaunchAgents on macOS
  • Package managers writing cron.d entries during legitimate app installs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","chef-client","puppet","salt-minion","cloud-init","rbenv","homebrew"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written unit/cron/plist and check whether it launches a binary named after a common tool from a user-writable path or references git.disroot.org; correlate the writer process back to a ruby require. 2) Contain: disable+remove the persistence artifact, kill the daemon, isolate the host, and rotate developer credentials/SSH/git tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep for the native binary drop (same name as the masqueraded gem tool), other hosts with the same unit/cron name, and any beaconing to git.disroot.org or its resolved IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","sh","bash","dash","zsh","gem","bundle")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ruby","gem","bundle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/","/etc/crontab","/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","sh","bash","dash","zsh","gem","bundle")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress wp2shell batch REST API pre-auth RCE exploitation (CVE-2026-63030/60137) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint /wp-json/batch/v1 (or rest_route=/batch/v1) that carry the batch-route-confusion + author_exclude/author__not_in SQL injection used by the wp2shell pre-auth RCE. Article-specific: anchors on the exact entry-point path plus the injected SQLi parameter and time-based payload tokens. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim article/PoC strings: entry path /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 (Code Block 1/2) plus the SQLi injection parameter author_exclude/author__not_in and time-based SLEEP() payload confirmed by the Searchlight write-up and the public detection PoC. Endpoint + non-GET method + SQLi token is very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://github.com/Senanfurkan/wordpress-cve-2026-63030 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-63030/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-party plugins/mobile apps that batch REST calls through /wp-json/batch/v1 (no SQLi tokens present, so the SQLi selection filters them)
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus/wp2shell.com checker) probing the batch route from known scanner IPs
  • Security researchers or the site owner testing exposure with the published PoC
  • WAF/CDN health checks that touch REST routes but not the batch endpoint with injection params
Suppression filter
| where not (src IN ("10.0.0.0/8") AND like(user_agent,"%HealthCheck%"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests to /batch/v1 from the source IP over the prior 24h; check scStatus (200 with post-shaped response body indicates the route-confusion succeeded) and confirm the target WordPress version is < 6.9.5 / < 7.0.2. 2) Contain: block /wp-json/batch/v1 and rest_route=/batch/v1 at the WAF/CDN, force the site to 7.0.2 (or 6.9.5), and rotate DB credentials if injection returned data. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host — look for web-daemon-spawned shells and newly written .php files under wp-content/ within minutes of the request.

| where csUriStem has "/batch/v1" or csUriQuery has "rest_route=/batch/v1"
| where csMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","PATCH","DELETE") or csUriQuery has_any ("author_exclude","author__not_in","SLEEP(","NOT IN")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=cIP, Method=csMethod, UriStem=csUriStem, UriQuery=csUriQuery, Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent, Site=sSiteName),

| project TimeGenerated, Host=CsHost, SrcIp=CIp, Method=CsMethod, UriStem=CsUriStem, UriQuery=CsUriQuery, Status=ScStatus, UserAgent=UserAgent, Site=CsHost)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress wp2shell Batch REST API Pre-Auth RCE Exploitation Attempt
id: 8f3b2c19-6d4a-4e21-9a17-3c5e8b1d7a02
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests to the WordPress core REST batch endpoint (/wp-json/batch/v1 or rest_route=/batch/v1) carrying author_exclude/author__not_in SQL injection tokens used by the wp2shell pre-auth RCE (CVE-2026-63030 + CVE-2026-60137).
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/unauthenticated-rce-in-wordpress-wp2shell
  - https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    - cs-uri-stem|contains: '/batch/v1'
    - cs-uri-query|contains: 'rest_route=/batch/v1'
  selection_sqli:
    - cs-uri-query|contains: 'author_exclude'
    - cs-uri-query|contains: 'author__not_in'
    - cs-uri-query|contains: 'SLEEP('
  condition: selection_path and selection_sqli
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate applications performing bulk operations through the REST batch endpoint (rare, and would not carry SQLi tokens)
level: high

Web server daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) spawning a shell or network tool — wp2shell post-exploit code execution AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm, apache2/httpd, nginx, or IIS w3wp/php-cgi) spawning an interactive shell or egress tool (sh/bash, nc/ncat, curl/wget, python/perl, cmd/powershell). Article-specific because the flaw yields arbitrary code execution under the web user with no plugin involved. Rationale: Article states the flaw 'chains into remote code execution' against a stock install under the web user; the highest-fidelity host signal for that is a WordPress web daemon (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) parenting a shell or egress binary — a parent+child pairing that is abnormal for a web server. Parent set is WordPress-specific, not a generic LOLBin template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress plugins that legitimately call exec()/shell_exec() (e.g. image optimizers invoking convert, backup plugins invoking mysqldump/tar)
  • WP-Cron or deploy hooks running via php-fpm that shell out to curl/wget for remote fetches
  • Server management panels (Plesk/cPanel) whose PHP workers spawn shells for admin tasks
  • CI/CD or WP-CLI automation executed under the web account during scheduled maintenance
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i","bash -c","sh -c","-e /bin","base64 -d","|sh","| sh","IEX","-nop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for reverse-shell/download syntax (/dev/tcp, nc -e, bash -i, curl|sh) and correlate the timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending php-fpm/worker child tree, and pull the box out of the load balancer. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by that PID (UC3) and outbound connections from the web daemon; capture bash history and /tmp for staged payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProc=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","perl","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New PHP file written into WordPress web root by a web daemon — wp2shell web shell drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts web shell persistence following the wp2shell RCE: a WordPress web worker (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp/php-cgi) creating a new .php/.phtml/.php5/.phar file under wp-content, wp-admin, or wp-includes. Article-specific because unauthenticated RCE in core is routinely followed by dropping an attacker PHP payload into the web-accessible tree. Rationale: WordPress web daemons should not author new PHP files in the web root outside of an update; pairing the web-worker writer (php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp) with a fresh .php under wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes is a high-signal web shell drop for a core RCE that runs as the web user. Web-root paths are WordPress-specific, not a generic file-write template. Cross-checked against: • https://slcyber.io/research-center/wp2shell-pre-authentication-rce-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.cryptika.com/new-wp2shell-rce-vulnerability-hits-millions-of-wordpress-sites-emergency-patch-released/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress core auto-update to 6.9.5/7.0.2 rewriting bundled PHP files (expected right now given forced auto-updates)
  • Plugin/theme installation or update from the admin dashboard writing PHP into wp-content/plugins or /themes
  • Caching plugins (WP Super Cache/W3 Total Cache) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php drop-ins
  • Backup/restore or staging-sync tooling repopulating the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "wp-cron" and FolderPath !has "cache" and not (FileName in~ ("object-cache.php","advanced-cache.php","db.php"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the created file — flag short files containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_REQUEST/$_POST/preg_replace(/e); compare the writer PID and timestamp against UC1 batch-endpoint requests and known update windows. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (do not delete before imaging), block web access to it, and isolate the host if the content is a shell. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files touched by the same PID/session, review access logs for GET/POST hits on the new filename, and check for scheduled tasks or wp_options/wp_users tampering.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7" or FileName endswith ".phar"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, WebDaemon=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/","\\wp-content\\","/wp-admin/","\\wp-admin\\","/wp-includes/","\\wp-includes\\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","php5","php7","phar")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("httpd","apache2","nginx","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-17 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A technical analysis of three chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Siemens ROX II OT switches that allow privilege escalation and persistent root access. The post Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Siemens RUGGEDCOM ROX II devices exposed to CVE-2025-40947/48/49 (firmware < V2.17.1) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II root cron table injection via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II xz utility misused as cat to read root-owned secrets (CVE-2025-40948)
Siemens RUGGEDCOM ROX II devices exposed to CVE-2025-40947/48/49 (firmware < V2.17.1) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Siemens RUGGEDCOM ROX / ROX II OT switches carrying the three chained zero-days that lead to persistent root access. This is the primary defensive action from a responsible-disclosure article with no in-the-wild IOCs: find and patch exposed devices to V2.17.1 before the chain is weaponised. Rationale: Uses the three exact CVE IDs disclosed in the article/advisories and the fixed firmware V2.17.1 as concrete grounding; DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities.CveId is a deterministic exposure match with near-zero FP. Cross-checked Siemens ProductCERT SSA-973901 and NVD. Cross-checked against: • https://cert-portal.siemens.com/productcert/html/ssa-973901.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/siemens-ruggedcom-rox-ii-exploit-chain-exposes-ot
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Device already scheduled for the V2.17.1 patch window but TVM scan predates remediation
  • Decommissioned/lab ROX II unit still inventoried by Defender for IoT
  • TVM CVE-to-asset mapping lag after firmware upgrade (stale SoftwareVersion)
  • Non-production spare switch on the bench flagged identically to production
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each hit is a live, in-service ROX II and read SoftwareVersion — anything below V2.17.1 is exploitable. 2) Contain: restrict network access to the device's web-management interface to a dedicated management VLAN/jump host and enforce MFA on ROX admin accounts (all three CVEs are authenticated) until patched. 3) Hunt: pull ROX II syslog/audit for the file-disclosure (xz) and root-cron persistence UCs below to check whether an exposed device was already touched.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2025-40947", "CVE-2025-40948", "CVE-2025-40949")
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2025-40947", "CVE-2025-40948", "CVE-2025-40949")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
Siemens ROX II xz utility misused as cat to read root-owned secrets (CVE-2025-40948) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the CVE-2025-40948 primitive: the root-privileged xz binary invoked with decompress-to-stdout flags to stream arbitrary sensitive files (shadow, private keys, config) like the Linux cat command. Article-specific because the file-disclosure vector is explicitly xz-as-cat, not a generic file-read tool. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit statement that xz is run 'with specific parameters to function like the standard Linux cat command' to read files as root; pairs the xz binary + decompress-to-stdout flags with sensitive-file targets so it does not fire on legitimate compression. Marked Low confidence as ROX II must forward auditd/syslog for the host-side query to have data. Cross-checked against: • https://cert-portal.siemens.com/productcert/html/ssa-973901.html • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/siemens-ruggedcom-rox-ii-exploit-chain-exposes-ot
ATT&CKT1003.008 T1552.004 T1005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decompressing an xz-compressed backup/log to stdout during troubleshooting
  • Firmware update tooling that streams xz archives containing config
  • Backup job piping xz -dc of an archived key store during restore
  • Support engineer using xzcat on a diagnostics bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (".xz", ".tar.xz", "backup", "/var/log/") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("/etc/shadow", "id_rsa", "/etc/ssh", ".key"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account/session that ran xz and confirm the target file is a secret (shadow, ssh/ssl keys, ROX/confd config) rather than a routine archive. 2) Contain: force-rotate any credentials, password hashes and private keys resident on the switch, and revoke the ROX admin session; block the source IP from the management interface. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for the feature-key command-injection follow-on and the root-cron persistence UC — file disclosure is step 1 of the chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "xz"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-dc", "--stdout", "-d -c", "--decompress", "--format=raw")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "id_rsa", "/etc/ssh", "/etc/ssl", ".key", "private", "/etc/confd", "/etc/rox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName == "xz" or SyslogMessage has "xz"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("-dc", "--stdout", "-d -c", "--decompress", "--format=raw")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "id_rsa", "/etc/ssh", "/etc/ssl", ".key", "private", "/etc/confd", "/etc/rox")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II root cron table injection via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) AIInstallation Low
Hunts CVE-2025-40949: the web-management task scheduler writing attacker-controlled commands into the device's root cron table for reboot-surviving persistence. Targets creation/modification of root crontab paths carrying network/reverse-shell commands on the ROX II Linux OS. Rationale: Grounded in the article's CVE-2025-40949 description of injecting commands into the 'system's root cron table' via the web task scheduler for reboot-surviving persistence; keys on the concrete root cron paths plus reverse-shell/download command tokens to separate malicious entries from routine scheduling. Low confidence pending ROX II file/audit telemetry forwarding. Cross-checked against: • https://cert-portal.siemens.com/productcert/html/ssa-973901.html • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/siemens-ruggedcom-rox-ii-exploit-chain-exposes-ot
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin scheduling a maintenance/backup job via the ROX task scheduler
  • Firmware/config-management tooling writing routine cron entries at provisioning
  • Monitoring agent installing a periodic health-check cron job
  • Genuine curl/wget-based update task added by an operator
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget", "curl", "/tmp/", "bash -i", "/dev/tcp", "mkfifo", "nc ", "ncat")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the new/modified cron entry — inspect the command for outbound download, reverse shell (/dev/tcp, mkfifo, nc), or /tmp payload execution, and identify the ROX account/session that created it. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron entry, kill any spawned child process/listener, revoke the admin session, and isolate the switch's management interface. 3) Hunt: confirm the full chain — check for the preceding xz file-disclosure and feature-key command-injection activity on the same device, and sweep other ROX II units for identical cron entries.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/spool/cron/crontabs", "/etc/cron.d/", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron/root")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility == "cron" or SyslogMessage has_any ("/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "crontab")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget", "curl", "/bin/sh", "bash -i", "/tmp/", "nc ", "ncat", "mkfifo", "python -c", "/dev/tcp")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor terminal RCE: web-server/PHP process spawns shell (CVE-2026-55579) AIExploitation High
Hunts the PHP/web-server process behind pheditor.php spawning an interactive shell or recon binary, which is exactly what the app's terminal feature does after an attacker logs in with the hardcoded default password 'admin'. Web servers legitimately almost never spawn sh/bash/cmd, so this is the highest-fidelity signal of terminal-feature RCE. Rationale: Anchored on Pheditor's terminal feature (PoC: action=terminal, command=`echo \`id\``) which makes the php/web-server user exec a shell; the web-server-parent + shell-child pair is inherently rare. Corroborated by CVE-2026-48030 which documents the same terminal command handler. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843 • https://github.com/pheditor/pheditor
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP application shelling out via exec()/system() for image processing (ImageMagick, ffmpeg wrappers)
  • Deployment/health-check scripts where php-fpm runs a shell one-liner
  • Composer or CI hooks invoked under the web-server account during deploys
  • Monitoring agents that fork whoami/uname under the httpd service account
  • Legitimate admin actually using the Pheditor terminal for maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","composer","healthcheck","/opt/deploy/"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the child process command line and the parent php command line (which often contains the pheditor.php script path); confirm the shell executed attacker recon (id, whoami, uname, curl). 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill the php/web-server process tree, and rotate the Pheditor password off 'admin' (or take the app offline) since default creds grant terminal access. 3. Hunt: review the web access log for the source IP's prior POSTs to /pheditor.php, check for webshell .php drops in web root and any modification of pheditor.php itself.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","php.exe","php-cgi.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python3","python")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe"))
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","/id","/whoami","/uname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pheditor Terminal RCE - Web Server Process Spawns Shell (CVE-2026-55579)
id: 8b1d2f6a-3c4e-4a91-9b77-2f0e1d6c9a51
description: Detects a PHP or web-server process spawning a shell or recon binary, consistent with Pheditor's terminal feature executing commands after default-credential login.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27

  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php'
      - '/php-cgi'
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/nginx'

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(php|php-cgi|php-fpm|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp\.exe)$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|id|whoami|uname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python3)|\\(cmd|powershell)\.exe)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Pheditor file-upload abuse: web-server process writes new .php webshell AIInstallation High
Hunts a PHP/web-server process creating or renaming a .php file (other than pheditor.php) in the web root, the expected outcome of abusing Pheditor's authenticated file-upload/editor to drop a webshell after default-credential login. A running web server writing brand-new executable PHP is a classic webshell-install signal. Rationale: Article names 'file upload' and 'file editor' as compromise vectors enabling arbitrary file write/webshell; the discriminator is a web-server process creating a NEW .php (excluding the app's own pheditor.php, covered separately). Path-agnostic so it works regardless of MAIN_DIR location. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://github.com/pheditor/pheditor
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application caching that compiles/writes .php (Twig cache, Smarty templates_c) under the web-server user
  • Composer/CI deploy writing vendor .php files as the deploy runs under the web account
  • CMS auto-update (WordPress/Drupal) writing plugin .php via php-fpm
  • Legitimate Pheditor admin creating a new .php through the editor for maintenance
  • Opcache/preload warmers touching .php files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\cache\\", "/cache/", "/templates_c/", "/var/cache/", "\\vendor\\", "/vendor/"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: open the newly written .php and grep for webshell markers (eval, system, passthru, base64_decode, $_REQUEST/$_POST exec); note file path relative to web root. 2. Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and reset the Pheditor password off default 'admin'. 3. Hunt: pivot on subsequent requests to the new .php filename in web logs, look for php spawning a shell (see terminal-RCE UC), and check whether pheditor.php source was also modified.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FileName !~ "pheditor.php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","php.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where TargetFileName !endswith "pheditor.php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor source tampering: modification of pheditor.php (hash rewrite / backdoor persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts any create/modify/rename of pheditor.php. The app's password-change routine writes the new SHA-512 hash directly into pheditor.php source, so an attacker with default-cred access can rewrite the hash to plant a persistent credential/backdoor. This surfaces both malicious source tampering and legitimate-but-risky in-source password changes for review. Rationale: Article pins the credential store at pheditor.php:11 (unsalted SHA-512) and states the password-change feature writes the new hash into the PHP source (lines 363-391); any write to pheditor.php is therefore high-value — either a backdoor hash-rewrite or a password change that must be validated. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://github.com/pheditor/pheditor
ATT&CKT1554 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin changing the Pheditor password (the app rewrites pheditor.php by design)
  • git pull / deploy updating pheditor.php to a new release
  • Editor/IDE atomic-save creating a temp then renaming to pheditor.php
  • Backup/restore tooling touching pheditor.php mtime
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet) redeploying the file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","ansible","puppet","ansible-playbook"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: diff the new pheditor.php against a known-good baseline for a changed PASSWORD hash (line 11) or injected eval/system/backdoor logic in lines 1-20; identify the writing process/user. 2. Contain: if the change is not an authorized password rotation, restore the file from a trusted baseline, isolate the host, and force a real password reset off default 'admin'. 3. Hunt: correlate with the source IP that authenticated to /pheditor.php, look for terminal-RCE shell spawns and dropped webshell .php files on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor default-credential exploitation traffic: POST to /pheditor.php from external source AIDelivery Low
Surfaces HTTP POST requests to /pheditor.php (the single-file app's auth + terminal + upload endpoint), plus any request whose query string carries action=terminal/upload/command/pheditor_password. For an internet-facing deployment still on the default 'admin' password this is the initial-access footprint. Hunting-tier because standard access logs don't capture the POST body that distinguishes the action. Rationale: Uses the article's fixed endpoint (/pheditor.php) and PoC parameter names (pheditor_password, action=terminal, command=) as the pivot. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty because HTTP access logs for a self-hosted PHP app don't ship to those EDR/cloud sources; Sentinel W3CIISLog and Splunk Web cover IIS/App Service/proxy telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843

Contain: if the host is internet-facing on default creds, take it offline or firewall /pheditor.php to trusted IPs and change the password off 'admin'. 3. Hunt: for the same source IP and host, pivot to endpoint telemetry for php spawning shells (terminal RCE), new .php webshell writes, and pheditor.php source modification.

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua with double-slash path traversal to secrets (CVE-2026-53713) AIExploitation High
Hunts EnvoyExtensionPolicy create/update whose inline Lua contains the exact double-slash bypass paths (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) that defeat the is_critical_path check in security.lua. This is the concrete exploit signature for arbitrary file read from the Envoy Gateway controller pod during Strict validation. Rationale: Uses the exact double-slash payload paths named in the advisory (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) scoped to the envoyextensionpolicies resource — legitimate Lua policies never reference these. Cross-checked GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f and the related GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/CVE-2026-22771/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team submitting a sanctioned validation/PoC policy to confirm patch status
  • Automated CVE-scanner or admission-controller test harness replaying the exploit manifest
  • A Lua policy that legitimately references /certs/ (single slash) mis-typed with a double slash by an operator
  • Backup/GitOps replay re-applying an old exploit manifest already stored in the repo
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !in ("system:serviceaccount:security-tools:cve-scanner") and UserAgent !has "validation-harness"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full requestObject for the flagged EnvoyExtensionPolicy and identify the submitting user/SA, source IP and userAgent; confirm the Lua references the double-slash sensitive paths. 2) Contain: delete the policy, rotate the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount token and any TLS keys reachable from the controller pod, and revoke the submitter's RBAC to create EnvoyExtensionPolicy. 3) Hunt: check the resource status/response for leaked token or file contents (see companion UC), and review kube audit for the envoy-gateway SA being used from unexpected sources afterward.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("//etc/passwd","//var/run/secrets","//proc/self/environ","//certs/")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), SrcIPs = tostring(User.extra)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - 'create'

source:kubernetes.audit @objectRef.resource:envoyextensionpolicies @verb:(create OR update OR patch) (*//etc/passwd* OR *//var/run/secrets* OR *//proc/self/environ* OR *//certs/*)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" "objectRef.resource"="envoyextensionpolicies" (verb="create" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")
| search requestObject="*//etc/passwd*" OR requestObject="*//var/run/secrets*" OR requestObject="*//proc/self/environ*" OR requestObject="*//certs/*"

Leaked SA token / file contents in EnvoyExtensionPolicy status (CVE-2026-53713 disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual secret disclosure: an envoyextensionpolicies audit record whose responseObject/status contains a JWT (service-account token), /etc/passwd content, or a PEM private key returned by the failed Strict validation. This confirms exploitation succeeded rather than just being attempted. Rationale: The related advisory confirms the SA token is 'returned in an error which will be displayed in the resource status'; eyJhbGciOi is the constant base64 prefix of a JWT header and root:x:0:0 is the invariant first line of /etc/passwd — both are high-fidelity content markers requiring RequestResponse-level audit. Cross-checked GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A policy legitimately referencing a JWT sample string in a comment (rare)
  • Audit policy not set to RequestResponse level so responseObject is empty (false negative, not FP)
  • Security testing that intentionally reproduces the disclosure in a lab cluster
  • A PEM string embedded in an unrelated but co-located config field captured in the same response
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked material from responseObject — decode the JWT to identify which ServiceAccount was disclosed and its namespace/audience. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/delete that ServiceAccount token (delete the SA's token secret / bounce the pod to force projection refresh) and rotate any disclosed TLS private keys; treat the token as compromised. 3) Hunt: search kube audit for that SA's token being replayed (new sourceIPs, verbs it does not normally perform) and pivot to the companion token-reuse UC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend RespStr = tostring(ResponseObject), StatusStr = tostring(ResponseStatus)
| where RespStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN PRIVATE KEY","serviceaccount/token") or StatusStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, ResponseStatus, RespStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua invoking os/io/debug file primitives AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for EnvoyExtensionPolicy manifests whose inline Lua calls filesystem/OS primitives (io.open, io.popen, os.getenv, os.execute, os.remove, debug.getinfo) — the building blocks any variant of this exploit needs to read the controller pod's files, catching payloads that use paths other than the four named in the advisory. Rationale: Reading a file from Lua requires io/os primitives; legitimate Envoy request-processing Lua manipulates headers/bodies and rarely touches io.open/os.execute, so their presence in a submitted policy is a strong pre-execution signal even when the payload uses a novel path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate advanced Lua filter that reads a mounted config file via io.open
  • os.getenv used to read a benign env var for routing logic
  • Developer testing a Lua snippet copied from a tutorial that includes os.time/os.date near os.execute
  • Vendor-provided policy template that legitimately uses debug for logging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Lua body from requestObject and determine whether the io/os call targets sensitive paths or is benign routing logic. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the policy and rotate controller credentials; if the cluster runs a vulnerable version, prioritise upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to the double-slash and status-disclosure UCs for the same policy name and submitter.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("io.open","io.popen","os.getenv","os.execute","os.remove","debug.getinfo")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous EnvoyExtensionPolicy submitter / suspicious policy name AIDelivery Medium
Profiles who creates EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources to surface rare submitters, and flags policy names containing exploit markers (poc, test, bypass, exploit, passwd). Because the exploit requires an attacker to create/patch the policy via the K8s API, unusual submitters are a leading indicator. Rationale: EnvoyExtensionPolicy objects are normally authored by a small, stable set of platform/GitOps identities; the summarize-by-submitter surfaces rare creators without a hard-coded allowlist, and the name markers catch dropped PoC manifests. Grouping/rarity is evaluated at rule level for Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux SA) creating policies — high count, benign
  • A developer genuinely naming a policy 'canary-test' or 'lua-test'
  • First-time onboarding of a new platform engineer who legitimately creates a policy
  • CI pipeline SA applying policies from a new namespace
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for any rare submitter or exploit-marker name, retrieve the policy body and check for Lua io/os calls or double-slash paths. 2) Contain: if the submitter is unexpected, revoke their create/patch RBAC on envoyextensionpolicies and delete the policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the submitter identity across other CRDs and namespaces for further unauthorized changes.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), PolicyName = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| extend SuspiciousName = PolicyName has_any ("poc","test","bypass","exploit","passwd")
| summarize Count=count(), Policies=make_set(PolicyName, 25), AnySuspicious=max(tolong(SuspiciousName)), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SubmitUser, UserAgent
| order by Count asc

Vulnerable Envoy Gateway version exposed to CVE-2026-53713 AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt that flags hosts/images running an Envoy Gateway version affected by CVE-2026-53713 (>=1.8.0-rc.0 <1.8.1, or <1.7.4) so the exploitable surface is remediated to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 before an attacker submits a malicious EnvoyExtensionPolicy. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the affected/fixed version ranges from the advisory (fixed >=1.7.4 and >=1.8.1). This is the only pivot expressible on Defender/Sentinel native telemetry since the attack itself lives in K8s audit logs; relies on container/software vuln assessment picking up the envoyproxy/gateway package. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched version mis-fingerprinted by TVM as vulnerable (stale scan)
  • An image tag pinned to a fixed digest but labelled with an old version string
  • Non-production/lab Envoy Gateway flagged alongside prod
  • TVM not yet ingesting the CVE definition (false negative, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.7.4 or in 1.8.0-rc.0..1.8.1 and that the instance accepts EnvoyExtensionPolicy submissions. 2) Contain: restrict RBAC so only trusted identities can create/patch EnvoyExtensionPolicy, and apply the Lua-docs Warning-section workarounds until patched. 3) Hunt: upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 and retro-scan kube audit for prior exploit attempts against the affected cluster.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Envoy Gateway ServiceAccount token reuse for anomalous K8s API actions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation hunt: the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway) performing actions it never legitimately performs — creating/deleting pods, exec/attach into pods, reading kube-system secrets, or touching cluster RBAC — which indicates the disclosed token is being replayed against the API server. Rationale: The advisory states the disclosed token can be used to 'read sensitive information from the K8s API Server'; the envoy-gateway controller SA legitimately manages EnvoyProxy infra in its own namespace but never execs into pods, reads kube-system secrets, or edits cluster RBAC — so those verbs under that identity are strong reuse signals. SA name/namespace confirmed from Envoy Gateway deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/operations/deployment-mode/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Envoy Gateway upgrade/migration job temporarily granting the SA broader RBAC
  • A future controller version that legitimately reads a secret in a shared namespace
  • Cluster admin impersonating the SA for troubleshooting (kubectl --as)
  • Backup tooling running under the same SA reading secrets broadly
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "envoy-gateway/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit compare sourceIPs and userAgent against the controller pod's normal client (in-cluster pod IP, controller userAgent); an external IP or kubectl/curl userAgent is high-confidence token theft. 2) Contain: rotate the envoy-gateway SA token immediately, cordon/quarantine any pods created by the SA, and review/revert RBAC changes. 3) Hunt: enumerate every action taken by the token since the disclosure event and check for new workloads, exfil connections, or additional credential reads.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), NS = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where SubmitUser == "system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway"
| where (Verb in ("create","delete") and Resource in ("pods","pods/exec","pods/attach"))
     or (Resource == "secrets" and NS == "kube-system")
     or (Resource in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings","clusterroles"))
| project TimeGenerated, SubmitUser, Verb, Resource, NS, ObjName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm installer spawns Python or script host (UAT-11795 Starland RAT) · [LLM] ClickFix mshta.exe silently executing remote HTA then dropping batch (UAT-11795 initial access) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PowerShell AMSI/ETW bypass reflection (UAT-11795 WLDR evasion) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Begun, the Patch Wars have
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] In-memory WLDR PowerShell C2 implant (fileless, no -File, unusual parent) · [LLM] Blockchain-anchored C2 fallback: non-browser process contacting polygon-rpc.com · [LLM] Connection to known UAT-11795 Starland RAT C2 / distribution domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CastleStealer/Starland RAT accessing browser credential stores and crypto wallets · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm installer spawns Python or script host (UAT-11795 Starland RAT) AIDelivery High
Hunts UAT-11795's supply-chain delivery where a trojanized installer for WebEx, Zoom, MobaXterm, DBeaver or FaceIT spawns a Python interpreter or scripting/LOLBin child that stages the Starland RAT. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact legitimate-tool installer names abused by this campaign paired with anomalous child processes those installers never legitimately launch. Rationale: Anchors on the exact trojanized-installer set (WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm/DBeaver/FaceIT confirmed across BleepingComputer, SecurityAffairs, gbhackers) as parent, paired with python/script-host children that these GUI installers never legitimately spawn — a two-predicate combination, not a bare process filter. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MobaXterm/DBeaver legitimately shelling out to cmd.exe or python for a plugin build task on a developer workstation
  • Zoom/WebEx auto-update helpers invoking cmd.exe for cleanup
  • IT packaging/repackaging of these installers via a wrapper that launches PowerShell
  • Security testing / EDR validation replaying installer-spawn behavior
  • A developer manually launching python from a terminal that was itself spawned by DBeaver
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/c update","autoupdate","uninstall"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child command line and SHA256; confirm whether the installer parent came from an official domain/signed publisher and whether the python/script child references a temp path, HTA, or base64 blob. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the python/script process tree, and quarantine the installer binary and any dropped .bat/.hta/.py artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same installer SHA256 across the fleet, look for follow-on mshta.exe, in-memory PowerShell (WLDR), and outbound connections to the campaign C2 domains and polygon-rpc.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("webex","zoom","mobaxterm","dbeaver","faceit")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentLower = tolower(ParentProcessName), ChildLower = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where ParentLower has_any ("webex","zoom","mobaxterm","dbeaver","faceit")
| where ChildLower has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\webex.exe'
      - '\zoom.exe'
      - '\ZoomInstaller.exe'
      - '\MobaXterm.exe'
      - '\dbeaver.exe'
      - '\FACEITClient.exe'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'

      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Webex.exe OR *\\webex.exe OR *\\Zoom.exe OR *\\zoom.exe OR *\\ZoomInstaller.exe OR *\\MobaXterm.exe OR *\\mobaxterm.exe OR *\\dbeaver.exe OR *\\DBeaver.exe OR *\\FACEITClient.exe) @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe)

ClickFix mshta.exe silently executing remote HTA then dropping batch (UAT-11795 initial access) AIDelivery High
Hunts the UAT-11795 ClickFix lure where the victim pastes a command that runs mshta.exe against a remote/HTA payload, which silently drops a Windows batch file and the trojanized installer. Article-specific because it targets mshta.exe launched from a user-shell parent (explorer/cmd) with a URL or scriptlet argument — the exact behavior Talos told defenders to monitor. Rationale: Talos explicitly advised monitoring mshta.exe execution and ClickFix; corroborating write-ups describe the HTA being run silently to drop a batch file and trojanized installer, so mshta with a URL/scriptlet arg or a user-shell parent is the high-fidelity signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html

  • Help-desk scripts using mshta for a UI prompt
  • Software packaging tools invoking mshta from cmd during install
  • Rare admin one-liners testing mshta connectivity
  • Legacy intranet portals delivering .hta over http
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\intranet\\","corp.local") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the mshta URL/scriptlet; resolve the domain and check reputation, and look for a batch file or installer written within 60s on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill mshta and children, and block the resolved domain at proxy/DNS. Step 3 (hunt): Search for the same URL across UrlClickEvents/proxy logs, and for subsequent python.exe (Starland RAT) or in-memory PowerShell on the host.

PowerShell AMSI/ETW bypass reflection (UAT-11795 WLDR evasion) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the AMSI and ETW tampering UAT-11795 uses before running its in-memory WLDR PowerShell implant. Detects PowerShell command lines containing the well-known AMSI reflection strings (AmsiUtils, amsiInitFailed) and ETW patching (EtwEventWrite, ntdll/etw provider disable), which precede fileless C2 execution. Rationale: Talos explicitly names AMSI and ETW bypasses as UAT-11795 tradecraft; the reflection strings (AmsiUtils/amsiInitFailed/EtwEventWrite) are the canonical, high-signal artifacts of that tampering visible in command lines and AMSI script capture. In-memory WLDR PowerShell C2 implant (fileless, no -File, unusual parent) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts UAT-11795's WLDR agent: a fileless PowerShell C2 that runs entirely in memory with a Runspace execution engine. Detects powershell.exe launched with -NoProfile/-NonInteractive/-w hidden but WITHOUT a -File or .ps1 reference, spawned by a non-standard parent (python/mshta/installer), indicating memory-resident script rather than a saved script. Rationale: Talos/corroborators describe WLDR as a fileless PowerShell memory implant with a Runspace engine; the discriminator is hidden/non-interactive PowerShell with NO -File/.ps1 (nothing on disk) spawned by the RAT's Python or the delivery LOLBins — expressed as a leftanti-style negative predicate rather than a bare PS filter. Correlation/negation shape, so Sigma omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-russian-speaking-threat-actor-uat-11795-targets-us-and-europe-with-novel-malware
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1620 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Login scripts / GPO PowerShell run hidden with -NoProfile from explorer
  • RMM tools (e.g. an agent) launching hidden PowerShell without -File
  • Software installers legitimately invoking inline PowerShell
  • Scheduled-task wrappers that pass inline -Command
  • Developer tools (VS Code, python venv activation) spawning hidden PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","taskeng.exe","svchost.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Grab the parent chain and any inline -EncodedCommand/-Command payload; a python.exe or mshta.exe parent with no on-disk script is high-priority. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and capture a memory image before reboot (the implant is memory-only). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with encrypted beaconing, DNS to polygon-rpc.com and campaign C2 domains, and prior AMSI/ETW tampering on the same host/session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| extend cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine)
| where cmd has_any ("-nop","-noprofile","-noninteractive","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden")
| where not(cmd has "-file ") and not(cmd has ".ps1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("webex","zoom","mobaxterm","dbeaver","faceit")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where tolower(NewProcessName) has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| extend cmd = tolower(CommandLine), par = tolower(ParentProcessName)
| where cmd has_any ("-nop","-noprofile","-noninteractive","-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden")
| where not(cmd has "-file ") and not(cmd has ".ps1")
| where par has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","webex","zoom","mobaxterm","dbeaver","faceit")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) @ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe) @CommandLine:(*-nop* OR *-noprofile* OR *-noninteractive* OR *hidden*) -@CommandLine:(*-file* OR *.ps1*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/(python|pythonw|mshta|wscript|cscript|webex|zoom|mobaxterm|dbeaver|faceitclient)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(-nop|-noprofile|-noninteractive|-w\s+hidden|-windowstyle\s+hidden)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/(-file\s|\.ps1)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Blockchain-anchored C2 fallback: non-browser process contacting polygon-rpc.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts UAT-11795's blockchain-anchored C2 fallback where the implant queries a Polygon RPC endpoint (polygon-rpc.com) to retrieve/refresh its C2 configuration. Detects connections/DNS to polygon-rpc.com and other blockchain RPC/explorer domains initiated by non-browser, non-wallet processes (powershell/python/mshta), which is anomalous for those binaries. Rationale: polygon-rpc.com is a confirmed campaign IOC and the Polygon RPC endpoint the article's blockchain-anchored fallback would query; scoping to non-browser/non-wallet initiating processes removes legitimate crypto-app traffic and makes the RPC contact high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1008 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's python script legitimately querying etherscan/polygon RPC for a DeFi project
  • Node/crypto tooling using rundll32-hosted helpers to reach an RPC endpoint
  • Blockchain analytics software with a non-browser agent
  • Security research detonations reaching blockchain APIs
  • A legitimate wallet CLI written in Python contacting polygon-rpc.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\venv\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "web3"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the initiating process and whether the host has any legitimate blockchain-development role; inspect the process command line and parent chain. Step 2 (contain): Block polygon-rpc.com and the observed RPC domains at egress for the affected host group, isolate the host if the process is powershell/mshta/python with no dev justification. Step 3 (hunt): Pull the retrieved payload/response, and hunt the same host for WLDR in-memory PowerShell, AMSI tampering, and the campaign C2 domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","etherscan.io","blockchair.com","api.blockcypher.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","etherscan.io","blockchair.com","api.blockcypher.com")
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where tolower(ActingProcessName) has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
    | project DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
  ) on DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High-fidelity IOC-match detection for direct connections or DNS resolutions to the UAT-11795 campaign infrastructure disclosed by Talos (eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com, zynaris.io, windowscreenrepairnearme.com, aipythondevs.com). Any endpoint or gateway contact with these domains warrants immediate investigation. Rationale: These six domains are the Talos-disclosed UAT-11795 infrastructure from the pre-extracted IOC set; a direct IOC match on DNS/network telemetry is inherently high-fidelity and needs no behavioral context. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pre-registered but now-sinkholed domain resolving to a research sinkhole IP
  • Threat-intel/EDR product itself resolving the domain for enrichment
  • An analyst manually browsing the domain during investigation
  • A domain later re-registered by a benign owner after takedown
  • URL-scanning services in the environment pre-fetching the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and host; determine whether the resolution was a real payload fetch vs. a scanner/sinkhole. Step 2 (contain): Block all six domains at DNS/proxy, isolate any host with a non-scanner process making the request. Step 3 (hunt): On confirmed hosts, hunt for the trojanized installer, mshta HTA chain, WLDR PowerShell, CastleStealer wallet access, and Remcos artifacts.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com","zynaris.io","windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com","zynaris.io","windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
